summary: For ages 5–7: children learn that many everyday foods come from rainforests — chocolate from cacao beans, bananas, shade-grown coffee, Brazil nuts — by starting from foods they actually eat and tracing each one backwards to the tree or plant it grew on in a hot, wet place near the Equator. The intended goal is a personal, memorable FOOD → PLANT → FOREST link, not manufacturing detail. The main proposal is a tap-to-zoom breakfast-table image; active matching/sorting and an end-check are preserved as alternatives with distinct purposes.
misconceptions: 'Chocolate is made in a factory / comes from a cow' — children conflate the shop or milk with the true plant origin (cacao beans).
'Food comes from the supermarket' — the shop is the end of the chain, not the source.
'Bananas/coffee grow in Britain' — not realising these need hot, wet tropical conditions.
'Nuts grow underground/in packets' — Brazil nuts fall inside heavy pods from giant rainforest trees.

activities.title: Tap a food, travel back to its rainforest tree
steps: Look at a familiar plate or breakfast table showing foods the child actually eats: a chocolate bar, a banana, a cup of coffee, a handful of Brazil nuts.

First guess the surprise flap question 'Where does chocolate REALLY come from?', then tap the chocolate bar and watch it zoom/flip into a knobbly cacao pod split open on a rainforest tree trunk, spilling pale beans, with the caption 'chocolate begins here, on a tree in a hot, wet forest.'
Tap the banana to travel to a towering tropical banana plant; tap the coffee to find red berries ripening in green forest shade; tap the nuts to see a giant emergent tree drop a heavy seed-pod.
Say aloud for one food: where it grows, that it grows on a tree or plant in a hot wet place near the Equator, and that the shop is the END of the journey, not the start.
Close the pictures, answer the flap question 'Where does chocolate REALLY come from?' from memory, then lift the flap to check your answer.
activities.insight: Some ordinary foods on my plate, like chocolate, bananas, coffee and Brazil nuts, began their life far away on trees or plants from hot, wet rainforest places, so my breakfast is connected to faraway forests.

activities.title: Match the food to the tree it grew on
steps: Drag each supermarket food (chocolate bar, banana, coffee, Brazil nut) onto the rainforest tree or plant it grew on.
Watch wrong matches bounce back and correct ones trigger a short animation from the growing form (cacao pod with beans, coffee berry, banana bunch, Brazil nut pod) to the food we buy.
After matching, say for one pair why that food belongs to that plant (e.g. 'chocolate comes from cacao beans in a pod on this tree').
activities.insight: Each everyday food can be paired with the specific rainforest plant it came from, and the growing form (bean, berry, pod) turns into the food we recognise.

activities.title: End check: sort and match rainforest foods
steps: Sort a set of foods into 'from the rainforest' versus 'not from the rainforest'.
Match each rainforest food to the plant it grows on.
Name at least three foods that come from rainforests, and explain that cacao beans grow on trees in the rainforest and are made into chocolate.
Pick a rainforest food you ate today or recently and trace it back to the plant it grew on.
activities.insight: I can recognise which everyday foods come from rainforests and explain the chocolate-from-cacao chain.

checkQuestion: Where does chocolate really come from — is it made in a factory out of nothing, or does it start as something growing in a rainforest? Tell me, and then tell me WHY chocolate is connected to rainforests.
checkAnswer: Chocolate starts in the rainforest: it's made from cacao beans that grow in pods on cacao trees in hot, wet tropical forests. The factory turns the beans into chocolate, but the beans come from a tree. Lots of everyday foods — bananas, coffee, Brazil nuts — come from rainforests too, so our food connects us to faraway forests.
